title: Subtraction with Borrowing for Grade 2: Step-by-Step (+ Free Quiz)
meta_desc: Teach subtraction with borrowing in Grade 2 the clear way: exchange a ten for ten ones, work column by column, and check by adding back. Free quiz inside.
excerpt: The moment a Grade 2 child meets 52 − 27, the fingers come out and the guessing starts. Here is the written borrowing method explained the way it actually clicks, with a free 8-question quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 52 − 27 in a column in front of a seven-year-old and watch what happens. Nine times out of ten they look at the ones column, see 2 on top and 7 below, decide 7 is bigger — so they simply do 7 − 2 and write 5. That single habit is the biggest hurdle in subtraction with borrowing for Grade 2, and it is the whole reason the written method has to be taught slowly and out loud, not just drilled. Borrowing is not a trick. It is place value doing exactly what place value is for.

In my experience teaching second-graders, the children who struggle are almost never bad at the arithmetic. They are fuzzy on one idea: that the 5 in 52 is really 50, five bundles of ten, and one of those bundles can be broken open into ten loose ones whenever the ones column runs short. Get that idea solid with real objects first, and the pencil-and-paper steps stop feeling like magic.

Why we borrow — it is all place value

Take 52. It is 5 tens and 2 ones. Now try to take away 7 ones. You only have 2 ones, so you are 5 short. Instead of giving up, you walk over to the tens next door, pick up one ten, and exchange it for ten ones. Now the same number 52 is written as 4 tens and 12 ones — nothing changed in value, we just repackaged it. Suddenly 12 − 7 is easy, and the tens column has 4 left instead of 5.

I always model this with bundles of ten straws held by a rubber band. Snapping the band and spilling ten straws onto the desk makes ‘exchange a ten for ten ones’ a thing children can see and touch. NCERT calls it regrouping; older books say borrowing; parents sometimes say carrying (which is really the addition version). Same idea, different label.

The step-by-step written method

Here is the routine I want a Grade 2 child to say aloud every single time, using 52 − 27:

  • Line up the columns. Ones under ones, tens under tens. Sloppy alignment causes more wrong answers at this age than the maths does.
  • Start at the ones, on the right. Always right to left. Look: 2 ones on top, take away 7. Not enough.
  • Borrow one ten. Cross out the 5, write 4 above it. Carry the ten across to the ones, so the 2 becomes 12.
  • Subtract the ones. 12 − 7 = 5. Write 5 in the ones column.
  • Subtract the tens. Now it is 4 − 2 = 2. Write 2 in the tens column. Answer: 25.

Notice the order that matters most: you decide whether to borrow before you subtract the ones, and you must remember to knock the tens digit down by one afterwards. Forgetting that second part — leaving the 5 as a 5 — is the other classic error.

A worked comparison

ProblemOnes columnBorrow?Tens columnAnswer
68 − 248 − 4 = 4No, 8 is enough6 − 2 = 444
52 − 272 becomes 12; 12 − 7 = 5Yes4 − 2 = 225
40 − 160 becomes 10; 10 − 6 = 4Yes3 − 1 = 224
73 − 453 becomes 13; 13 − 5 = 8Yes6 − 4 = 228

Run through the table with your child and ask, for each row, one question before anything else: ‘Is the top ones digit big enough?’ If yes, no borrowing. If no, borrow first. Making that a spoken decision every time is what builds the habit.

Check the answer by adding back

This is the step almost everyone skips, and it is the most valuable one. Subtraction and addition undo each other, so the answer plus the number you took away should return the number you started with. For 52 − 27 = 25, check: 25 + 27 should equal 52. Add them — 25 + 27 = 52. Correct. If it does not come back to 52, something went wrong, usually the forgotten tens reduction.

I would make adding-back non-negotiable for the first month. Yes, it doubles the work. That is the point — a child who checks catches their own mistakes and stops depending on you to mark every sum.

The classic mistakes to watch for

  • Smaller-from-bigger in each column. Doing 7 − 2 instead of 12 − 7 because 7 looked bigger. This is the number-one error — catch it early.
  • Forgetting to reduce the tens. Borrowing the ten but leaving 5 in the tens column instead of 4.
  • Borrowing when you did not need to. Crossing out a perfectly good tens digit out of habit, even when the ones column was fine.
  • Messy columns. Ones drifting under tens, so the child subtracts the wrong pairs.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz built around exactly these ideas — deciding when to borrow, the exchange step, and checking by adding back. Let your child work each one on paper first, then read the explanation together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives plenty of column-subtraction questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Subtraction with Borrowing Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on column subtraction that needs regrouping. Work each one on paper, pick your answer, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: The ones need borrowing: 2 becomes 12, so 12 − 7 = 5. The tens drop to 4, and 4 − 2 = 2. Answer: 25.

questions.q: In 43 − 18, what does the ones column become after borrowing?
questions.explanation: You borrow one ten, so the 3 ones become 13 ones. The ones column is 13 − 8 = 5.
0 ones cannot take 4, so borrow: 10 − 4 = 6. The tens go from 6 to 5, and 5 − 2 = 3. Answer: 36.

questions.q: Which subtraction does NOT need borrowing?
questions.explanation: In 56 − 23 the top ones digit 6 is already bigger than 3, so no exchange is needed.

questions.q: After borrowing in 74 − 46, what is the new tens digit on top?
questions.explanation: You borrow one ten from the 7, so it drops by one to 6. Then the tens column is 6 − 4 = 2.
5 cannot take 7, so borrow: 15 − 7 = 8. Tens drop to 7, and 7 − 4 = 3. Answer: 38.

questions.q: You worked out 63 − 28 = 35. How do you check it by adding back?
questions.explanation: Add the answer to the number you took away: 35 + 28 should give 63. It does, so 35 is correct.

questions.q: A shop had 90 pens and sold 55. How many are left?
questions.explanation: 90 − 55: borrow so 10 − 5 = 5 ones; tens go from 9 to 8, and 8 − 5 = 3. Answer: 35 pens.

faq.q: What is the difference between borrowing and regrouping?
faq.a: They are two names for the same step. NCERT and newer textbooks say regrouping; older books and many parents say borrowing. Both mean exchanging one ten for ten ones so the ones column has enough to subtract from.

faq.q: Why does my child do the smaller digit minus the bigger one?
faq.a: Because 7 looks bigger than 2, they flip it to 7 − 2. Fix it by always asking ‘is the top digit big enough?’ first — if not, borrow before subtracting. Practising with straws or coins makes the exchange concrete.

faq.q: Should I teach borrowing before or after mental subtraction?
faq.a: Teach the written column method here once single-digit subtraction is secure. Mental shortcuts are a separate skill for another day — mixing both at once tends to confuse a Grade 2 child.

faq.q: How can my child check a subtraction answer alone?
faq.a: By adding back: the answer plus the number taken away should return the starting number. For 52 − 27 = 25, check 25 + 27 = 52. If it does not match, they know to redo it — usually a forgotten tens reduction.
